title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01

pages.label: 001_Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01 Part 1

blocks.x: So we're all ready to start. I'll give my voice. This is Bill Russell and we're down at the home of Mealy Barnes and Paul Barnes on Louisa Street. Do you want to give your name Mr. Mealy Barnes, Emile Barnes? Mm-hmm. What is your full name? My full name is Emile Barnes. Any middle name or initial? Mealy Barnes. Oh. That's Mealy.

pages.label: 002_Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01 Part 2

blocks.x: They're going again. You were talking, was it Buddy Petit you said you played with?

Yeah, I played with Buddy Petit out there. We worked out on Shantown, Louisiana. We worked out there and the band continued to see Buddy Petit, the boys on trumpet, we had Ambrose on trombone, we had John Moreau was on banjo, Hudson was on bass.

pages.label: 003_Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01 Part 3

blocks.x: The The Can you tell again about this is a real interview Mealy Barnes for a half hour and we'll continue with that story about how Joe Oliver did he play the the band? Well Joe, Joe was in the brass band then. I just remember when you went away in the army. Howdy

pages.label: 004_Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01 Part 4

blocks.x: It's going again. We'll talk to Paul for the next half hour.
Well, what do you say if I give you a short interview from the time I left for Celestan?
Fine, that'll be good. Yes, bring it up to date from Celestan.
Well, you're ready now?
Yes, okay, you can go ahead with your life.
I'll say, I started playing music in 1919. September, I'll never forget the gate. September the 3rd. The saxophone, just one month. Well, we formed a little band, Lawrence Murad and so forth.
That's to get back to that, that was the E-flat alto.
With an E-flat alto.
I was going to ask once, somebody told me most of the fellas started with the C melody. Remember those old days when everybody used the C melody, I thought, but you didn't get in on that.

No, in fact, no one used the C melody around New Orleans. I don't know any otherwise, because they always figured that a C melody was too soft for a band. And so orchestration was put up though, with the music for C melody, but we never did use it.
I know a lot of people bought those and they wouldn't even have a part for them in late years anymore.

Yeah, late years they cut it. They changed the orchestration. Orchestration used to be put up for shell and oboe and all that stuff as time went to change. But anyway, we formed this band called Lawrence Murad and I. It was the original Diamond Band. And we had Bush Hall on the trumpet. That's the time I'd taken a wife. We weren't making much money. And then I went with Kid René's band. That was up until 1922. And I went with Kid René's band. I wanted to get me, especially Simon Murad was in the band. So I quit Kid René's band and I went with the Maple Leaf band. I've heard of the Maple Leaf. That was Willie Pajot and Willie Bontane and Oak Gasper, that bass player, Vic Gasper. Vic was on trombone.
Yeah, on trombone.
Willamita Bontane and me, Paul, Globone, were playing sax. Now, uh... Is that the one? Yeah, this is the one.

That's the card that Ralph has here. Is that one you got from Fess? Uh-huh. Original Maple Leaf novelty jazz orchestra. Octave Gasper, manager. 1728 Marais. Music furnished for all occasions. And Victor Gasper, that's the right way to spell their name, is it G-A-S-P-A-R-D. Uh-huh. And he was on Allen Street. That's about where he lived all his life, wasn't he? That's right. 1525.
That's right.
You see that, Mary? I didn't... Excuse me.
I didn't work with them long. Maybe just about three weeks or so. Yeah. And I left and I went with the Tuxedo Band.
Oh, let's see.

That fellow, Dave Dupas, he was an insurance collector. And he used to worry me, worry me, but John, the Tuxedo Band, that's a great band, and John would... Well, Simon was playing with the Kid René Band, he quit the band and he went with the Tuxedo Band. So Simon and John Marara both went with the Tuxedo Band, and I wanted to get over there. So I left Maple Leaf Band and I joined the Tuxedo Band, that was in 1923. Who was the actual leader?
Celestan or Ridgely? No. Bebe Ridgely. That was the manager of the band.

Yeah. But Celestan was the leader, the trumpet player, he was the leader, but Bebe Ridgely was the manager of the band. He took care of all the business. Did they have a violin in those days? Well, they were just about dying out. Pierron was the only one that I know of, Lef and Robichaux. They were the only ones that I can remember that played in, but all the rest of the head died out by that time. Paul. Do you know of anyone else? I think all of them Paul.
Is that Paul Dominguez?
Paul Dominguez. Paul Dominguez. Was he still playing then? Yeah. Well they were the only ones because they were dying out then.
Paul Dominguez, Peter Bauer, and I was on band.

Well that was the year, we played out at Tranchinas out in the lake when I joined Tuxedo Band. We were taking Pierron's band's place. I played a couple of jobs with Pierron's band also. Well Pierron went to New York at that time and we'd taken his place until he came back. We worked there a year.
I don't want to interrupt you, but I don't want to miss this about you took some lessons from Lorenzo Teo, you say. He helped you with the sax or clarinet or both?
Oh no, with the saxophone. With the sax. I actually didn't take any lessons from anyone on the clarinet. You see, no more than Miele gave me.
That's Miele helping you.

Helping you with the clarinet. But I got some great advice from Tartarella from the Boston Conservatory of Music when I was in the Navy. Yes. And I would practice and he'd sit down and tell me the different things and he'd see to it that I would smooth out my tones and so forth. It made quite a great difference in my playing.
I was wondering about Teo since he's not living of course and we never found very much information about Teo. Do you remember much about how he played and what he told you when he helped you or what

he was like? For his playing, actually I think that he was one of the greatest players we had here at that time. Lorenzo Teo, his tone and all was so smooth. But mostly when I would take lessons with Lorenzo Teo, he was always tipsy. Sometimes I couldn't get my lesson. He was always tipsy. Somebody told me he liked wine a lot.
Is that it or what? I didn't know.
I never know what he drank. But he stayed high.

Oh well, something else. As I say, I know almost nothing about him. Some people told me that it might have been his father or his uncle they were talking about, the old Lorenzo or Papa, that they talked a little bit with an accent, a French accent. Did young Lorenzo still have a French accent? He did. He did too.
At that time, he the young fella, he did have a French accent. But he taught me and Bonnie Bigard taking lessons from the Teos also, but from the daddy, I think.
Yes, I did.
I don't think it was Lorenzo, but he was from the daddy. Anyway, when Piro and them returned in 1924, the Tuxedo band came out. And you heard some of the recordings that we made.
Yes, we have.

Black Rag and so forth. But there was a confusion came up between Ridgely and Salastair concerning some of the money. The band broke, broke up. Salastair quit the band. In fact, the band actually didn't break, but Salastair quit the band. But John Marrera and Simon Marrera came to me and said that they wanted to get Salastair and make another band, Tuxedo band. So I was young, I followed them, and so that was the beginning of the original, Salastair's original Tuxedo band. That was in 1924. Now that made, they had two Tuxedo band, they had Ridgely's Tuxedo band and Papa Salastair's original Tuxedo band. Well finally Ridgely's Tuxedo band faded out and left just Papa Salastair's Tuxedo band in the field. And we did pretty good. So I composed a number and called it My Josephine. And that number made such a hit, that was really the making of Papa Salastair's original Tuxedo band.

The most popular number I think that he ever made. Well I was going to ask, we talked to Ridgely for about an hour or so one day, and he told us some of that story about how they split up too. And how they first started by wearing tuxedos even on the brass band they had on the street. I hadn't known that.
Yeah we always wore tuxedos. You always wore tuxedos?
Always, yeah.
Collin tie, white shirt, and tuxedo. On the dance job.
Yeah that's right. Did you ever play in any of the Tuxedo brass band?
Oh yeah, yeah I played.
Did you ever play in the time when they really wore tuxedos on the street?
No, no.
You never, no I didn't. You weren't in that band?
No, that was before my time. But I played in the later one, when Willie Paggio and they was playing with us then.
Okay don't let me interrupt you.

Well the Tuxedo original original tuxedo band we did pretty good but we had times we had a pretty rock we wasn't making anything. At one time I quit the band and I formed another band and the band was good and we called it the Young Tuxedo Band and we'd get work from them. I was always growing from band because I wasn't doing anything much. So I left that band and I went with Sidney Daysbeens band. We played out on the Island Queen, you see, around 25.
Well where did you go on that boat? We didn't go anywhere.
We just played over at the head of the, right the river. Right it was here.
I thought it was mostly up around Cincinnati and Ohio.
I never did go away with the boat.
You didn't go away?
No we played right there every night. Well did the Streckfus boat? But the boat would go up the river a piece. Yeah I know. And come by.
I didn't know they played here in New Orleans. I thought only the Streckfus boat played here most of the time. Like the St. Paul and Sidney and the JS and those boats.
I never played on that but I played on the President. See I played that boat.
In those days then when the Island Queen, that was a rival line, did they have two dances? I just kind of. I mean two boats here at the same time?

I just don't remember if they had two at the same time. But I know what we played, I played the Capitol on the Capitol and with Papa Solis there. Not regular, we played jobs on the Capitol. But I did play regular on the Island Queen in Sidney. And that was around 1925. But I didn't play it, stayed there too long. I left the band and went back with Papa Solis there and band and stayed there until 27.
I didn't know that, that bothers me about that boat being here. Was that winter time or summer?
Usually in the cold weather.
In the cold weather when they played.

So, in the, up until, I went back with Solis there, last of 25 and I stayed until 27. And by that time King Oliver had heard that record, My Josephine and hearing all the work on the saxophone. And right down to Manuel Perez and found who it was and Manuel told him who it was. And in through Manuel, I went with King Oliver. And that was in 1927.
Where was he when he located you then? He was in Chicago.

In Chicago. Yeah, King Oliver was in Chicago. But I didn't meet him in Chicago. He left Chicago. He was going on a job in New York. But we met him in St. Louis. St. Louis. And the ones who left here together was Willie Foster, Red Allen, and myself. See, we left together and we went to St. Louis. Willie Foster is Pop Foster's brother.
Yes, we talked to him up and he's in Baton Rouge. We saw him last January. Last January.

Well we went with King Oliver. Let's see, I think I can remember some of the names in that band. It was pretty long ways back. But on trumpet there, they had King Oliver. They had a trumpet player called Gray. So far I can't remember his name. He was Gray and Red Allen. It was three trumpets. On trombone we had one, we had Kid Ory on trombone. Now on bass we had a fellow, but his name was Buford. That's all I can remember. Buford, heavy dog. Buford, he was a bass player. On saxophone we had Omar Simeon. I think he passed away.
Just a week and a half ago.
And Bonnie Bigard and myself. They had rumors that we were the best sax section in New York at that time.
You went on to New York band with them? With that section.

And on the percussion we had on piano, Louis Russell and Paul Barbaran on drums. But the band didn't have any success. We stayed there and we worked at the Savoy Ballroom. We had no more than about two weeks and whatever came up, King Oliver came out. He didn't seem, he could get enough money. So he had offered to go to the cotton club and that was his great mistake. He wouldn't accept it. And that was King Oliver's downfall. Because he didn't think there was enough money in it and he wouldn't accept it. So Duke Ellington accepted the job. And the Duke Ellington band was broke up at that time and he was putting men together. He had Otto, a fellow on saxophone, and he was in need of saxophone players so he got the big odd from King Oliver's band, because our band was split up around New York. So he got the big odd to play saxophone.
That's when Barney went with him.

And yeah, Barney Big Odd went with him. And Duke Ellington was looking for me for saxophone, but he couldn't find me. So instead of getting me he got Johnny Hodges. Now Simeon left and he went to Milwaukee and then back he joined Earl Hines band. So Louis Russ, I was around doing anything. I was playing around with different bands, a fellow called Wilkins, a piano player, and Edgar Dow, a piano player, Jinger Young, Richard Cheatham from Cleveland, Ohio. I played a gig with Chick Webb's band. You know, a different band. I didn't belong to any regular band, but I played around with some of the greatest around New York and I was well respected, especially a man from King Oliver's band. So finally I went, Louis Russell recommended me, and I went with Jelero Martin. Now if you notice how the read section split, Barney Big Odd went with Duke Ellington, Simeon went with Earl Hines, and I, Paul Barnes, goes with Jelero Martin. So King Oliver didn't have any band. So King Oliver was playing around just like we did with different bands around New York. So he did get a band and he did some recording. See I've never recorded with King Oliver. You never did record? No, I recorded, it's a record I recorded with Louis Russell's band. Johnny Hodges and I, we worked together. But I just can't remember the name of that number, you might get it sometime, but it was Louis Russell's band. But King Oliver went on the road and he had Dave, a fellow who played trumpet, I think that was his cousin or nephew or something.
I believe I heard it, Dave Nelson.

Yeah, Dave Nelson. Well Dave Nelson made some arrangements for King Oliver. He did arrangements. Well during that time I was playing with Jelero Martin. And that was up until 1929, or the middle of 1929, Jelero Martin had a failure. His band from New York, he had a wonderful band, one of the best I've ever played with. They wouldn't go so we got different men and it's a long story but what we went through. But that's the last I know of Jelero Martin. That was in 1929. I don't think he lived much longer after that.
He went I think down to Washington, different places.

That's right. Well when he came back I played with, that's when I worked with Wilkins. We played at Quag Long Island for about six months and we had the famous Honey Brown singing with us. The girl that was to make that picture Hallelujah, she got sick and couldn't make it and they got Ninna Mae McKinney in her place and she got fame. Honey Brown she passed off. But anyway that was in 1929. It was six months.

Before you go on, I wanted to ask a little bit about Joe Oliver. How he was playing. Was he as good as before? I mean was he getting worse with his teeth or could he still play real well? What did you think of it?
He could play real well then.
Still play real well?

Real well then. And then later I'll come to the part where he began to fail. So after leaving Quag, after that job was up, then it was up to 1930. You see I played around with different bands up until 1931. I was playing with Richard Cheaterman in what you call a taxi dancing school they called up there. Then King Oliver came back with the band and asked me to make a trip with him. That was in 1931. Well John Marrero was to go on the trip but he was in bed with the union. He didn't make the trip. So in 1931 we had a contract with Frederick Brothers and we left New York, I think it was in May, to go to Wichita Kansas. I mean yeah Wichita Kansas they had Frederick Brothers. One of the longest rides I ever had in my life, halfway across the United States in a bus. Three days we were riding. Well we got over there and we were very much disappointed because we were supposed to get fifty dollars a week. But they wouldn't give us, but then one man said he wouldn't pay but forty dollars a week because King Oliver couldn't play the records when he was supposed to play because Dave Nelson, he had gotten in bed with King and he took all his arrangements. So King hit out on the road without any arrangements. And then the man said well we represent you to play these records but the new band he had couldn't play the records. So that cut us down. Well we did pretty good and the depression was on pretty strong then. It was pretty strong. Things got so bad that the man actually couldn't pay forty dollars a week. And then when they said when they cut the band down to fifty dollars a week King Oliver lost half of his good men. They all went back to New York. So he got another bunch of fellas and then when the man wanted to cut it down to thirty dollars a week then they left. So things was pretty bad so I told Simon at that time they had King Oliver had sent to New Orleans and got Simon Marrero. So I told Simon that I think I'm going to go back to New Orleans. That was the end of 1931. I said around Christmas time. I said I'm going back to New Orleans. Simon said yeah you do pretty good back in New Orleans. So I left King Oliver's band but when I left his band then his band was just gone to nothing. Everybody had left just had about five or maybe six or seven piece out of a fifteen piece band left. And they just playing a little job around which he wasn't doing anything. So I came to New Orleans and I got here and one of the saxophone players came down with me Walter Dennis. His name was he came down to New Orleans but things wasn't too good in New Orleans and Walter Dennis went back. I stayed around New Orleans and I worked around with different bands. I played with Mealy, Spain and with Abby Williams, George Williams and many others. It takes a lot of time to call them all. I have it all marked down to Willie Pajos, Melody Boys and so forth.

Some of this book I believe did you once loan this to Walter Allen? Yeah, I did. And I think he published that in an article, some of it in the record changer. I guess you got that paper that time. Wow. Called the King's Saxophone, remember that article.
I didn't get it. You didn't see it. I have it. You don't have it now.
We have it in Tulane. I'll bring the copy down and let you do that sometime.
I certainly would like to see that.
Yeah. Which he tells about all those times when they didn't get paid hardly anything. Some nights and now they...

Well anyway, in 1932 I was around New Orleans. I wasn't doing anything much around there. So I met my cousin, who's Baptiste. He said, my son Alex Ruschon is out in Lake Charles. He said, they got a good band out there. He said, why don't you go out there with them? Because Alexis had asked for me. He was a saxophone. He was my scholar and he was a good saxophone player. So I told him, I think I will. I'd go on out there. So I goes on out to Lake Charles. And I joins with that band. And they call it the Syncopators. They called it. That was the name of the band. Well we had a big fellow that was the leader. Oh by the way, I forgot to mention one more man in King Oliver's band. I hate to leave him out. Clarence Black.
Who was a violin?
He was a violin player. He was a violin in 1927 when we went to New York. I forgot to mention him.
St. Louis.

Yeah, to St. Louis from New York. But anyway, I finished telling you. They called this band the Southern Syncopators. And they had Alan Prairie, the big 330 pound man. He was, all he did was directing. He looked good in front of the band. And we had D.D. on trumpet. D.D. Pierce?
D.D. Pierce, yeah.
He would sing A La Ba. D.D. Yeah.
And we had. Well by the way, who do you think wrote that? Where was the first time you ever heard that?

D.D. Well, I'll tell you the facts of the thing. There's nobody around New Orleans wrote that. The, the, the, as far as I can, the man who composed it, I don't know his name, but he used to call him the Mayor of Pompon. That's all he said, he was the Mayor of Pompon. Yeah. And he used to sing that A La Ba.
I think it came out in the Creole country, I don't know, that's right. Yeah, that's right.
So, uh, D.D.
The Cajun country is what I meant to say, over that way.

D.D. heard him sing that and D.D. picked it up from him. Yeah. But D.D. didn't get the thing right, you see. Now I'm going to give you an idea how he'd go. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. That's where the Mayor of Pompon added. Yeah. But D.D. got it mixed up. D.D. came out. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. Yeah, he got it wrong and it just spread like that. So, well anyway, we had Nellie Lutcher, that was our piano player, and I can forget her father's name, he was our bass player, and a fellow called Joe, so far back and I can't remember, he was a drum player. And we had a fellow called Al playing saxophone. He left and went to Chicago. And Shelly LaMell, I don't know if you've heard of him.
No, I don't think so.

Well he's a pretty nice trumpet player. He was playing trumpet with us, Shelly LaMell. And we were quite a hit around Lake Charles. So the fellow said, well, Barnes, he said, Paul, he said, let us use your name. He called it the syncopated. He said, let us, you wouldn't mind if we use Paul Barnes? He said, you just come from New York with a big band from King Oliver, and that would be good when people hear it's Paul Barnes Band. I said, well, okay, if you want to use that name, you can go ahead and use it. So they changed the name to Paul Barnes Band. So I said, well, my name is so well known, I said, if we go through New Orleans, we would make quite a hit. So we brought the band to New Orleans and we played up at the Elk's home there, which was the Bull's Club. Yeah. The place was packed. It was a Paul Barnes Band, and that was the first of New Orleans here in El Aba, and the musicians was up there like that. And these New Orleans musicians can really pick up something. And they heard that, and from then on all the bands pick it up. But when they found out that it wasn't a copyright, and there's two of them tried to have it copyright, I don't think they succeeded. It was Burbanks and Ricard. And I think the government found out that they both was fighting over it thinking nobody getting anything of it. It's just traditional. Well, we played around with the band, and I got some things lined up here how the band was made, and that was in 1932. There was Shelley Lamelle, Joseph Pierce, trumpet player, Nellie Lutcher was on the piano, and on bass we had Chester Zardes. Oh yes. Yeah. And Alex Rouchon, that was a cousin of mine, he was on saxophone. Paul Barnes on saxophone, and Alfred Wilson, that's a tenor saxophone player's name. Alan Parade was the director, and Eldris Joe, that was our drum player. Well that band did pretty good. We made a tour all the way out to Mississippi and so forth, and I stayed there for 32 and 33, and we weren't making so much, so I left the band after playing in 32, and to 33 I came and I tuned home of Louisiana.
Yeah.

You see? And we're taking a job for a fella called Vincent Lepresto, a Paul Barnes band. Well we played for Vincent Lepresto through 33, and we were getting three dollars a night a man, and we would play two nights a week so that we made six dollars, and strange as it sounds, that six dollars was plenty of money at that time in 33, because some people wasn't, if they could make a dollar, I'm telling you, they would do good. They had people around there and some in the bread lines, and six dollars was, I used to walk down, it actually cost us 17 cents a day for our food, and we had all we wanted to eat. We would cook together, and you know that would be about a dollar and something a week, that we would, and we had plenty to eat with that, and I'd feed other people, and then we'd have extra money aside, you know, to buy and spend with the ladies and things around there. But there was a lot of confusion there, because that job, as cheap as that job was, there was musicians was grabbing at that job as if it was a thousand dollar a week job. You wouldn't imagine that thing was going on there. And then when we got to Richard Jones, piano player, come there, he came there and he was a pretty tough fella to get on. He wanted to take over everything. And he saw the band and showed the fellas that if he had the band in charge he would take the band away, but there wasn't anything away, you know. At that time, there just wasn't nothing.
Was that the songwriter, Hermione Jones from Chicago? I mean he came from here, but he wrote things like Trouble in Mind, do you remember? Was that the same one?
What's that said his name was? Richard Jones. Yeah, Richard Jones. Yeah, that's the same Richard Jones. He had quite a name.
Did he limp a little bit? Yeah, that's right. Piano player. I didn't know he was down here. I didn't know he came back.

Yeah, he came down here and he pulled those boys and so they got me out the band for a while. And so they fought so much over the band, I just quit and I left the band to go. I quit the band. After I quit the band, the band just went down. So I joined the band with Walter Johnson. Had a fella they called Walter Johnson. So I joined with Walter Johnson's band and we did pretty good work around there. And we got the job at the American Legion that Gabriel had the job there for about ten years and we got the job from him at the American Legion. And everybody around there was crazy about Paul Bones' band. And when we left that just practically ruined Vincent Lopresto's place, you see, because the people stopped going there and they started coming over to the American Legion where we were playing. And that band just went on through. Well I stayed with Walter Johnson until 1934 and things wasn't so good. By that time King Oliver sent for me. And I was back again with King Oliver. Then, you understand? Well, 34 I went, I met them in Paducah, Kentucky. And, uh, let me see if I'll have the, yeah. I could give you the lineup of the men. We had, uh, I met them, we had a fella called Selma Payne. He was a saxophone player. And we had Buddy Harrell. He was a trumpet. We had a fella called Herman Elkins. He came from New York. He was a trumpet. He was the one that came all the way from New York with King. And this Herman Elkins, he was a trumpet player in the same band that Cab Calloway had taken over. And he was playing with them at that time. And we had a fella, uh, Leonard Phillips. He was playing trumpet. And King Oliver was playing trumpet. And trombone, we had a fella called Otto Jones. We called him Pete for shorts. And piano, a little short fella called Charlie Turan. And on drums we had Deebo Mills, Demit Mills. Deebo Demit Mills, that was a drum player. And bass we had Andrew, Dan Andrews on bass. The guitar was Bernie Cobb. And we had a director, Billy Coleman was a director. And a songster we had Doris Duff. That was a wonderful songster. That boy could sing. He didn't chant anyone when you hear him sing. I never forget that.
Where did most of those people come from? Any certain part of the country? They weren't from New Orleans, I guess. No, no.

They, they, the only New Orleans person in this, that I've just called was, excuse me, King Oliver and me. King Oliver. But they all come from all different parts of the country. Some from Kentucky and New York, you know. It's all over. Yeah, all different places. Well I was very happy to get into that band. It really sounded good. The band was good. But to my disappointment, the band, things were just bad. I didn't make any more. You want to stop that now? I'm running. Well you want, I didn't, I wasn't making any more with that band than I was with the other
little bands around home and down here.

Some nights we'd play with, you know, I'd come from all different parts of the country. Some of them come from all different parts of the country, some from Kentucky and New York, you know. Right in your book there from that time. Yeah. From that time. Yeah.
From that time.

Yeah. I was just, I wasn't making any more with that band than I was with the other little bands around home and down here. Some nights we'd play, we'd make two dollars and maybe on the other nights we'd get a dollar sixty-eight cents a piece. That's what they, some nights, look, as much as, each is eighty-five cents a piece and it was just tough.
Right in your book there from that time.
From that time. Yeah. I'll tell you the rest after you. Well. That's the last tape you got.
No, see, we want to find out, go ahead, another half a minute on here.

Well, anyway, I'll make this short for you. That was in 34, I stayed with King until 1935 and during that time we had lots of trouble, buses break down. I read about that, yeah. Sometime that we'd almost go over the accident, I liked it, went over the hills and we had men that was quitting and no one would stay with the King. I loved the old King so much, I just wouldn't, wouldn't, I wouldn't let him down. I just stuck with him, see, when all was leaving. And King, he looked like he wasn't too worried. He admired me so much. As long as he had me with him, he seemed to be satisfied. Okay.
Okay. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
